title: The Professor Who Never Joined Facebook
author: Cal Newport
wiifm: Ericsson and Greene both quietly assume something most working days no longer provide: long stretches of uninterrupted thought. Today we follow Cal Newport, a computer scientist who built his career on refusing to be reachable, and the people whose habits he studied, from Carl Jung in his stone tower to Bill Gates in a lakeside cabin. You will learn why concentration is becoming rare just as it becomes valuable, what a glance at your inbox really costs, and four practical ways to build depth into a week that is already full of other people's demands.

b: Calvin Newport was born in 1982 and grew up in New Jersey. He was a technical, organised boy, and in high school he and a friend set up a small web design business. He went on to Dartmouth College to study computer science, and there he became interested in a question that most students never ask out loud: why do some people get far more done than others, without seeming to work longer hours?

He started interviewing the strongest students he could find, and while still an undergraduate he wrote a book of study advice based on what they told him. The answers kept pointing the same way. The best students were not the ones who spent the most time at their desks. They were the ones who concentrated hardest while they were there.

Newport took a doctorate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, finishing in 2009, and joined Georgetown University in Washington as a computer science professor. Along the way he made a choice that looked eccentric even then. He never opened a social media account. No Facebook, and later no Twitter. He was publishing research papers, writing books and running a popular blog, and he was convinced that the time and attention he had protected was the reason.

Deep Work, published in January 2016, is his attempt to explain why. It is part argument, part manual, and part collection of portraits of people who arranged their lives around concentration. The first portrait he paints is of a Swiss psychiatrist and a pile of stones.
ch.cap: Student Newport works late in a snowy Dartmouth library

b: In 1922 Carl Jung bought a plot of land on the upper shore of Lake Zurich, at a village called Bollingen, and the following year he began to build a round stone tower. He was a busy man with a large clinical practice in Zurich. About a decade earlier he had broken bitterly with Sigmund Freud, and he was now trying to build a whole new school of psychology out of the wreckage.

Over the years he added to the tower. Later in life he kept a private room in it, and he carried the key himself. Nobody else went in without his permission. When he stayed there, he would start the day with a couple of hours of writing that nothing was allowed to interrupt.

Newport's point is that Bollingen was not a holiday home. It was infrastructure. Jung had worked out that the thinking his new ideas needed could not be done in the gaps between patients. It needed a room, a key and a closed door. And the ideas he developed in those years, about archetypes, the collective unconscious and the shape of a life, became some of the most influential in twentieth century psychology.
ch.cap: Jung stacks stones for his tower at Bollingen

b: Newport's definition of deep work is deliberately narrow. It is professional work done in a state of distraction-free concentration that pushes your thinking to its limit. Done well, it creates new value, improves your skill, and produces something that is hard to copy. Its opposite is shallow work: logistical tasks that do not demand much thought, often done while distracted, and easy for someone else to do.

Notice what that excludes. Answering twenty emails thoughtfully is not deep work. Nor is a good meeting or a day of competent firefighting. All of these may be necessary. None of them makes you harder to replace.

The whole book hangs on one claim, which Newport calls the deep work hypothesis. The ability to do deep work is becoming increasingly rare at exactly the same time it is becoming increasingly valuable, so the few who cultivate it will thrive. Two trends are colliding. The tools of modern work, instant messaging, open-plan offices and the expectation of a reply within the hour, are designed to interrupt. And the work that machines and cheaper rivals cannot easily take over is precisely the work that needs long, hard concentration.

Newport names the winners of this economy. There are people who can work creatively with intelligent machines, there are superstars whose best work can be copied and spread everywhere for nothing, and there are the owners of capital. You probably cannot become a venture capitalist. But the first two routes both depend on the same two abilities: learning hard things quickly, and producing work of real quality at speed. Both are deep work abilities, and neither can be built in fifteen-minute pieces between notifications.
ch.cap: Pings scatter the office; one worker goes deep

b: Newport offers a formula that is almost rude in its simplicity. High-quality work produced equals time spent multiplied by intensity of focus. It is rude because it means that someone working twenty undistracted hours can beat someone working sixty fragmented ones, and most of us prefer to believe that hours are hours.

His illustration is the young Theodore Roosevelt at Harvard in the late 1870s. Roosevelt's days were absurdly crowded with boxing, rowing, natural history, a busy social life and the early research for a book on naval history. The time left for coursework was a fraction of his classmates'. His method, drawing on an account by the biographer Edmund Morris, was to choose a task, give it a fixed window, and attack it so fiercely that nothing else could get in. Newport calls these Roosevelt dashes.

You can run one today. Take a task you have been nursing for a week, estimate honestly how long it needs, cut the estimate until it feels uncomfortable, set a visible timer and go. The deadline does the work that willpower usually fails to do.

The modern version is the organisational psychologist Adam Grant, who became one of the youngest tenured professors at the Wharton business school. Grant batches. He packs his teaching into one part of the year so the rest is clear for research, and during research periods he alternates between being openly available and being completely shut away. His remarkable publication record does not come from superhuman hours. It comes from hours that are not sliced up.
ch.cap: Young Roosevelt dashes across Harvard, timing every task

b: The most useful research in the book is also the quietest. In 2009 Sophie Leroy, then a business school researcher at the University of Minnesota, published a paper with the memorable title Why Is It So Hard to Do My Work? She had discovered what she named attention residue.

When you switch from one task to another, your attention does not switch cleanly. Part of it stays behind, still turning over the first task, and that leftover attention makes you worse at the second. The residue is heaviest when the first task was left unfinished. People in her experiments who switched before completing a task performed less well on the next one.

The practical implication is sharper than do not multitask. A thirty-second glance at your inbox is not a thirty-second cost. You have dropped an unfinished obligation into your working memory, and it goes on charging rent for some time afterwards, whether or not you reply. Repeat that every quarter of an hour and you have built a working day in which you are never fully present at anything.

There is a hopeful footnote, published after Deep Work. In 2018 Leroy and Theresa Glomb reported in the journal Organization Science that when people were interrupted, taking a moment to write a brief plan for how they would resume the unfinished task reduced the residue and improved their performance on the interruption. The mind, it seems, will let go of something not when it is finished, but when it trusts there is a plan.
ch.cap: An unread email trails her into the next task

b: Newport is firm that willpower is not the answer. It runs out, and relying on it is a losing strategy. The answer is routines and rituals that make the decision in advance. He offers four ways of organising a life around depth, and asks you to choose honestly.

The monastic approach cuts out shallow obligations almost completely. The novelist Neal Stephenson is the example: for years his website explained that he does not answer email, because his time is already spoken for by the novels. The bimodal approach divides life into clear blocks, long stretches of total depth, a day at a time or more, alternating with ordinary availability. Jung at Bollingen is the model.

The rhythmic approach makes depth a simple daily habit at the same time each day, such as the first ninety minutes of every morning. For most people with a business to run, or a placement rota to work around, it is the only one of the four that survives contact with real life. The journalistic approach fits depth into any gap that appears, switching into concentration at a moment's notice. Newport warns that this takes years to learn, and that beginners who try it first usually conclude that none of this works.

He also describes the grand gesture: an expensive, dramatic change of setting that tells your own mind the work matters. Stuck on the final Harry Potter book, J. K. Rowling checked into the Balmoral Hotel in Edinburgh, reportedly paying around a thousand pounds a night, and finished it there in 2007. Bill Gates took twice-yearly Think Weeks alone in a cabin with a bag of reading, and in May 1995 he sent Microsoft the memo called The Internet Tidal Wave, which turned the company towards the web; it is often linked to one of those weeks. The money is not the point. A big enough commitment makes abandoning the work feel more absurd than doing it.
ch.cap: Deep hours blocked in ink; Balmoral's one lit window

b: To make depth actually happen, Newport borrows a management framework called the Four Disciplines of Execution. Focus on a small number of wildly important goals. Track the inputs you control rather than the results you do not. Keep a visible scoreboard. And review it regularly. His own scoreboard is a card on his desk where he tallies hours of deep work, circling the days a real milestone falls. It is childishly simple, and it works for the same reason a wall chart works.

He asks you to schedule every minute of your working day, not as a prison, but to force yourself to see what you are actually choosing. You will rewrite the plan constantly as reality interrupts. The discipline is in having had to decide. You will also discover how badly you underestimate how long things take.

The other half is the shutdown ritual. At the end of the day you review every open commitment, make sure each has a plan or a place in your system, and then say a fixed phrase. Newport's is schedule shutdown, complete. After that, work is over until morning. It sounds like theatre. But it rests on exactly the mechanism Leroy and Glomb later measured: the mind releases unfinished tasks when it trusts a plan exists. The ritual is how you make that promise credible to yourself.

He also practises what he calls fixed-schedule productivity. He stops work at around half past five and works backwards from that limit, refusing commitments that would breach it. A hard stop sounds like a limit on output. In practice it is a ruthless filter on what you agree to.
ch.cap: Another tally mark, then: schedule shutdown, complete

b: Newport's attack on social media got the headlines, and it is more interesting than the caricature. He does not say these tools are worthless. He attacks what he calls the any-benefit mindset: justifying a tool because it offers some conceivable benefit, while ignoring entirely what it costs. By that standard you would adopt everything, which is roughly what has happened.

His alternative is the craftsman approach. Identify the two or three activities that matter most to your goals, and adopt a tool only if its positive effect on those particular activities clearly outweighs its negatives. He suggests an experiment. Stop using an optional tool for thirty days, without announcing it. At the end, ask two questions. Would the month have been noticeably better with it? Did anyone notice I was gone? If both answers are no, you have your decision.

The final rule is to drain the shallows. Shallow work cannot be eliminated, but it can be budgeted. Decide what share of the week administration, email and routine calls may take, and defend the rest.
ch.cap: Phones glow down the carriage; one man reads a book

ch.h: What the book does not prove
b: Be clear-eyed about the evidence. Deep Work is mostly argument and well-chosen story, not controlled study. Jung, Rowling, Gates and Grant are chosen because they confirm the thesis. We are not shown the many disciplined, early-rising tower-builders who produced nothing of note. The attention residue studies are real and carefully done, but they were run in laboratories on artificial tasks, which is a long way from proving that an interrupted Tuesday costs a business a quarter of its output.

Newport even supplies his own best counter-example. Jack Dorsey, while running both Twitter and the payments company Square, worked in an almost entirely shallow way, constantly interrupted and deliberately visible. Newport's answer is that a senior executive's job is different, a decision-making machine fed by constant information. That is probably right, and it weakens the thesis more than he admits. In some roles the most valuable work really is fast, shallow and relational, and the book never draws that boundary clearly. Answering a client within the hour may be the job.
What survives is the part you can test on yourself in a fortnight. Uninterrupted blocks produce work that interrupted hours do not, and the difference is large enough to notice.
ch.cap: Notifications strike like lightning over a crowded desk

b: Newport kept building on the argument. Digital Minimalism followed in 2019, A World Without Email in 2021 and Slow Productivity in 2024, and he still has no social media accounts. He became, a little ironically, one of the best known voices on the subject in the world, largely through books and a podcast he produced in long, protected blocks of time.

The lesson of the week so far is starting to lock together. Ericsson told us skill is built by effortful practice at the edge of your ability, with fast feedback. Greene told us the apprenticeship is long. Newport makes the plain structural point that follows: you cannot do either if your day is shredded into pieces.

Jung needed a tower. Rowling needed a hotel suite. Most of us need something far cheaper: a fixed ninety minutes, a closed door, a phone in another room and a card on the desk to tally the hours. The point is not that you must live like a monk. It is that the work which matters most will not happen in the gaps. You have to build it a room.
ch.cap: Door shut, phone outside: ninety deep minutes at dawn

take: Concentrated work is valuable because it is hard to copy. Ask of any task whether someone cheaper could do it while half watching their phone.
Twenty undistracted hours often beat sixty fragmented ones. The fastest gain is fewer interruptions inside the hours you already have.
A glance is never just a glance
Checking your inbox leaves an unfinished task in your mind that drags on what you do next. Batch checks at set times instead.
When you must switch tasks, write one line on where you will pick up. It reduces the residue the unfinished task leaves behind.
For anyone running a business, the rhythmic approach, the same block at the same time each day, is the one most likely to survive real life.
Keep a visible count of deep work hours rather than outcomes. Inputs move daily and can be corrected; results move quarterly.
Review every open commitment, give each a plan or a home, then declare the day finished so your mind can let go.
Judge tools by the vital few
Adopt a tool only if it clearly helps the two or three activities that decide your success, and test optional ones by dropping them for thirty days.
recall: What is Newport's deep work hypothesis?

That the ability to do deep work is becoming rarer at exactly the time it is becoming more valuable, so the few who cultivate it will thrive. Interruptive tools make it scarce, while the hardest-to-replace work needs it.
What is attention residue, and what did Leroy and Glomb find helps?

When you switch tasks, part of your attention stays on the unfinished first task and harms performance on the next. Their 2018 study found that writing a quick plan for resuming the interrupted task reduced the residue.
Name Newport's four philosophies of depth and the one he warns beginners against.
Monastic, bimodal, rhythmic and journalistic. He warns beginners away from the journalistic approach, switching into depth whenever a gap appears, because it takes years of practice.
Why does a shutdown ritual work rather than being mere theatre?
The mind holds on to unfinished commitments until it trusts they are accounted for. Reviewing every open task and giving each a plan satisfies that, and the fixed phrase makes the promise credible.
What is the biggest weakness in the book's evidence?

It relies on well-chosen stories of successful people rather than controlled studies, and the residue research was done in laboratories. Newport's own example of Jack Dorsey shows that in some roles fast, shallow work is the valuable work.
note: Based on Deep Work and public accounts of Newport's career. Jung's Bollingen tower and private room are described in his Memories, Dreams, Reflections. Leroy's 2009 paper is in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes; the resumption-plan finding is Leroy and Glomb, Organization Science, 2018, published after the book. The link between Gates's 1995 memo and a specific Think Week is often repeated but loosely documented, and Rowling's room rate is a press report.
words: Interchangeable with something else of the same kind, so that one unit can easily replace another.
Newport's shallow work is fungible: anyone cheaper could do it while half watching their phone, so it never makes you hard to replace.
Lacking a plan or focus, passing from one thing to another without real attention.
A day sliced by notifications produces desultory work, the opposite of the intense, single-minded effort Newport calls deep.
A private, protected place where someone can be undisturbed.
Jung's locked room in his tower at Bollingen, with the only key in his pocket, was a sanctum built for thinking.
Having two distinct modes or peaks rather than one blended average.
Newport's bimodal approach splits life into long blocks of total depth alternating with ordinary availability, as Jung did.
Peculiar to one person, unusual and individual in a way others do not share.
Newport's refusal to open any social media account looked idiosyncratic for a young computer scientist, and he credits it for his output.
stories: In 1922 Carl Jung bought land on the upper shore of Lake Zurich, at a village called Bollingen, and the next year began building a round stone tower. He had a large clinical practice in Zurich and had recently broken bitterly with Freud. Over the years he added to the tower, and later kept a private room there whose key he carried himself. Nobody went in without his permission. When he stayed, he began the day with a couple of hours of writing that nothing could interrupt. Newport's point is that Bollingen was not a holiday home. It was infrastructure, built because the ideas Jung needed could not be done between patients.
The hotel suite that finished Harry Potter

Stuck on the final Harry Potter book, J. K. Rowling did something extravagant. She checked into the Balmoral Hotel in Edinburgh, reportedly paying around a thousand pounds a night, and finished the book there in 2007. The price comes from a press report, so treat it as roughly right rather than exact. Newport calls this a grand gesture: an expensive, dramatic change of setting that tells your own mind the work matters. The money is not really the point. A big enough commitment makes walking away from the work feel more absurd than doing it, and that tips the balance on the mornings willpower would fail.

At Harvard in the late 1870s, the young Theodore Roosevelt had a ridiculous schedule: boxing, rowing, natural history, a busy social life and early research for a book on naval history. The time left for coursework was a fraction of what his classmates had. Drawing on the biographer Edmund Morris, Newport describes his method: choose a task, give it a fixed window, then attack it so fiercely that nothing else could get in. Newport calls these Roosevelt dashes. The lesson is his formula in action: output is time multiplied by intensity, so a short, ferocious hour can beat an afternoon of half attention.
biz: Newport concedes that in some roles fast, shallow response is the job, and answering a homeowner's enquiry quickly is part of treating them well. So do not make everyone deep. Put first response to Google, Bing and Facebook leads on a clear rota with agreed hours, and give yourself a fixed ninety-minute rhythmic block each morning, phone in another room, for the work only you can do: compliance files, SEO content, lender relationships. Keep a tally card of deep hours and one output, such as SEO pages published per week. Check monthly that lead response times have not slipped.
Resume notes and a shutdown for every case

Debt advisers are interrupted constantly, and an unfinished case leaves attention residue that drags on the next caller, who may be in real distress. When switching mid-task, write one line in the CRM saying exactly where to resume. At the end of each day, run a shutdown: every open case must have a next action and a date before anyone logs off. Measure the number of open cases with no next action at close of day, aiming for zero. It cuts residue for staff, and under Consumer Duty it means no client quietly falls through the gaps.
connects: Adam Smith noticed in his pin factory that workers lost time passing from one sort of work to another, an early observation of the switching cost Sophie Leroy later measured as attention residue.
Marcus Aurelius wrote of retreating into his own mind as a quieter refuge than any country house, the inner version of Jung's tower at Bollingen.
Ericsson's purposeful practice demands full attention, which is only possible inside the uninterrupted blocks Newport sets out to protect.
recap:
Cal Newport was born in nineteen eighty-two and grew up in New Jersey, an organised boy who ran a small web design business in high school. At Dartmouth he asked a question most students never voice: why do some people get far more done without working longer? He interviewed the strongest students he could find. The answer kept coming back the same. They were not at their desks longest. They concentrated hardest while they were there.

He took a doctorate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and became a computer science professor at Georgetown. Along the way he made an odd choice. He never opened a social media account. He believed the attention he protected was why he could publish papers and write books at once. In twenty sixteen he explained it in Deep Work.

The book opens with a stone tower. In the nineteen twenties Carl Jung built one on the shore of Lake Zurich, and kept a private room inside whose key only he carried. He wrote there each morning with nothing allowed to interrupt. It was not a holiday home. It was infrastructure for thinking.

The first big idea is that depth is rare and valuable at the same time. The tools of modern work are built to interrupt, while the work that is hardest to copy needs long, hard concentration. Shallow work, the easy logistical kind, can be done by anyone.

The second idea is a formula. The quality of work equals time multiplied by intensity. The young Theodore Roosevelt at Harvard had a crowded life, so he gave each task a fixed window and attacked it ferociously.

The third is attention residue. The researcher Sophie Leroy found that when you switch tasks, part of your mind stays behind, especially if the first task was unfinished. A glance at your inbox is never just a glance. Later work showed that writing a quick plan for resuming helps the mind let go.

The fourth is that willpower runs out, so build routines. Newport offers four styles, from the monk who answers no email to the rhythmic habit of the same block every morning, which is the one most busy people can keep. End the day with a shutdown ritual, so open loops have a home.

Be honest about the limits. The book is argument and well-chosen story, not controlled study, and for some jobs, fast and shallow really is the work.

Still, try it for a fortnight and you will feel the difference.

The work that matters most will not happen in the gaps. Build it a room.
